493.t: Katrina strikes while he is in Japan
493.s: He was in Japan recording Concerto in F with Roberts and Ozawa when Katrina hit. His family evacuated to Jackson, and he describes the shock.
493.q: I must say though, that I think that Katrina probably impacted me the most, because of this – really, overall, I think that all of us were very fortunate, but it impacted me the most, because my parents were lucky, because in the neighborhood that they were

493.s: He thinks the musical lineage survived, citing gigs with Kermit Ruffins that December. Livelihoods and logistics suffered more.
493.q: Honestly, I don’t think it did anything in terms of music lineage. There’s some logistics that maybe got affected, in terms of business things that got affected. There was somebody that was talking about how there were different musicians that weren’t on the scene, that came in. They may have taken…

493.t: The city's neighborhoods and spirit after the storm
493.s: Asked about lost neighborhoods, he says the city's spirit will stay. Newcomers learn local food and music, and mixed-income housing replaced projects.
493.q: You know what? I honestly think that the city – it is my belief the city, it’s still going to be – I don’t know. I think it’s going to be, the more things change, the more things remain the same. I think that there will be – I just think that the overall spirit of the city is not going to change.

493.s: They stayed four months in Jackson and about a year in New York before returning to the repaired house. He reflects on staying spiritually steady.
493.q: We were in Jackson for about four months. Eventually we went to New York and went there for about a year. Then – but during that time we were in and out of New Orleans, seeing about the place. After about a year we were able to come back to New Orleans and live in the house that we live in now. But…

493.s: Brown raises the Dodds, Batiste, Jordan, Johnson and Barbarin families as examples of passing music through families.
493.q: Yeah. There’s also the Barbarin family.

116.t: Katrina's effects and Snug Harbor reopening
116.s: His uptown house stayed dry; Snug Harbor returned in October 2005 and the Saints boost.
116.ch: Katrina, race and New Orleans culture
116.q: No. See, this is – the uptown section, there was maybe about four feet of water in the street, which wasn’t enough to come into our house. We have an electric gate, and the box on the gate, that water cooked it. It was finished.

116.t: Recording resumes; Po-Boy festival; musicians come and go
116.s: Chat after interruption, then how hurricane affected musicians.
116.ch: Katrina, race and New Orleans culture
116.q: Yeah. Oak Street Po-Boy Festival, where all of these – there’s Po-Boys all up and down the street. I might go this year. I’ve never been. But I might just go down there. For the most part, New Orleans is a different kind of place, but not – because a lot of people still say, “How did the hurricane…

116.t: The Musicians' Village and the music center
116.s: He explains Branford and Harry Connick Jr.'s music center.
116.ch: Schools today and the Marsalis family
116.q: I’m mostly a consultant. I’m – that’s basically it, because I am not teaching. I may do some teaching, but for the most part, when it finally does open, there’ll be people that are teaching. I might stick my nose in a little bit here and there.

116.t: Life in Cajun country, Patois, and the call from Al Hirt's band
116.s: His wife disliked the town, he explains Patois, and after moving back to New Orleans he was called to join Al Hirt.
116.ch: Teaching and the Al Hirt band
116.q: Patois. That’s like some people say broken French. But that’s really what it’s called Patois. And they may say Cajun French. The essence of that language is that it’s very idiomatic so to speak. For example, there are no tenses. Like if it’s French and you want to make a statement, there are…

960.t: Plans, and his house in Algiers after Katrina
960.s: He describes Algiers Point, evacuating to Florida, and returning to find his house under leaves but intact.
960.q: After this I have to get back because the CEO of my school — well obviously I’m from New Orleans so you know about the transition that we’re going through. I was fortunate I didn’t lose my house. I live in a section of town that was actually was settled before New Orleans, it’s called Algiers. Some…

960.t: Loss and recovery in New Orleans after the storm
960.s: Family homes lost, musicians leaving, the city's history and rebuilding, and lost photographs.
960.q: of my house and that was it, you know, decorative tiles on my roof. That was it. I mean I was thankful. I mean in relation to everybody else who lost everything. My parents lost their houses, my sisters lost their houses, only one brother, believe it or not who lived in a part of town that really…

960.s: Realness in music and fundamentals being lost; Yvonne Bush as a band director who taught many New Orleans musicians.
960.q: Yeah. Somehow we can get back to — I don’t know see for me music is just real. It has to have a certain, not a surrealness about it but a realness about it, that can make you feel something, really make you feel something. And I hope that we can regain that. Because truly I can tell you there was…

888.t: Personal Katrina damage and rebuilding efforts
888.s: Her house was flooded and wind-damaged; she describes displaced colleagues and the musicians' village and Ellis Marsalis Center.
888.q: Well not as dramatic as some people. But I did have the flooding to the extent that we had to gut everything, take out all the walls, even the ceiling, the flooring, because of the water, and had wind damage. Part of my roof was in the driveway and all of that. But that’s able to be repaired. It’s…

888.t: Little competition among New Orleans musicians after Katrina
888.s: Returning musicians are glad to see each other, so there is joy rather than competition.
888.q: I don’t know so much as competition, I don’t know. I don’t think there’s competition because we don’t have very many musicians back in New Orleans yet. Because everybody, we’re so happy to see each other and we’re so happy to hear each other that we’re not competing with each other. You know the…

1007.t: Uneven recovery in the Lower Ninth Ward and saying both things about New Orleans
1007.s: He describes a Lower Ninth Ward high school still in temporary buildings against the quickly rebuilt Vietnamese community. He says the city is both not back to normal and ready for visitors.
1007.ch: Hurricane Katrina and New Orleans today
1007.q: might have moved back to New Orleans to help rebuild their own city. I mean there’s all sorts of things and dynamics of it that are not hard to understand, but at the same time it’s disconcerting to realize that our country, for all the greatness of our resources, on two fronts has not embraced our…

1007.t: Katrina: his best clarinet survived while he was in California
1007.s: He was in California working when the flood came and had left his best instrument in the apartment, barely above the water. He returned in early October 2005 to salvage.
1007.ch: Hurricane Katrina and New Orleans today
1007.q: Almost everything. Yeah. Not quite everything. I could have lost that. It wasn’t where it should have been. It wasn’t with me. It was in the apartment.

530.t: Evacuating to Baton Rouge; the flooded house
530.s: Evacuating to Alvin Batiste's house and the state of his flooded home.
530.q: Yeah I had to go to Baton Rouge with Alvin Batiste. He was living in New Orleans, he was working at a house in New Orleans and his home was in Baton Rouge. So we evacuated to his house. We had about twelve people in his house at the beginning. And eventually I got me an apartment I think the second…

530.t: Music appreciation classes, Katrina and retirement
530.s: Teaching music appreciation, finding students related to Bechet and Picou, and retiring when Katrina closed the music department.
530.ch: New Orleans families, lifestyle and retirement
530.q: Well and that’s what I want it to do. And you know the main thing about it, there’s some people I see say, “man, you still teaching school? If I had all the years you had I’d have been retired a long time ago. I say, “man I enjoy what I’m doing.” I didn’t go to school to sell insurance. I haven’t…

696.t: Playing at the St. Mark's Center benefit after Toni Morrison
696.s: Evacuated to Georgia and New Jersey, he plays a gig for poets and writers in the East Village that feels like a New Orleans church.
696.q: my grandson, and I played a gig the following weekend in the East Village at this St. Mark’s Center. And the feeling and the love that was in that center at St. Mark’s was I felt like I was in the church in New Orleans because it was more a thing of poets and writers who came together to pay homage…

696.t: Kerr's Katrina losses, family and hopes for New Orleans
696.s: He was luckier than relatives who lost homes; worried about his daughter and his son and daughter-in-law in Iraq, and hopes the people restore the city's spirit.
696.q: Yeah I didn’t lose my home like my sister, my daughter, my relatives, my closest friends and everybody that I know, really had twelve, fifteen feet of water and some parts of it were just blown away. My house was elevated. I’m in a section of the city that’s supposedly called a “no flood zone” but…

851.t: Katrina, gentrification and the loss of New Orleans' culture
851.s: He recounts his angry letter to a journalist claiming the city is back, the Hastert remark, leisure time as the source of creativity, and the post-Katrina housing changes.
851.q: Oh, I’m sorry, you’re right. So I wrote this scathing response saying that you know I mean listen, after Katrina happened the then-speaker of the house Denny Hastert actually said, “New Orleans is going to be too expensive to rebuild. If people want to hear jazz they can go to Walt Disney World.”…

851.t: What is New Orleans music: playing underwater and humid pianists
851.s: He calls New Orleans music an attitude, shaped by humidity and sea level, describes pianists like Toussaint and Booker, and laments gentrification.
851.q: I know. Is it Al Hirt? Is it the Neville Brothers? Is it Mannie Fresh? Is it Pete Fountain? What is it? It’s like it’s not a style it’s an attitude of playing music under water. Because in New Orleans we’re under water. Danny Barker used to say that. That’s why trumpet players from there, that’s…

583.s: Her caseload grows from 500 to 1500 musicians, and renting without pay stubs is a barrier.
583.q: Again, that really... We kind of exploded because of Katrina. There was such a need. We went from 500 musicians a year to 1500. It wasn’t just one family would be one case. You’d find someone, they’re in a dome somewhere, they need an apartment. Try to rent an apartment when you don’t have a pay…

583.t: Tracking down scattered musicians through WWOZ
583.s: WWOZ's David Friedman relays callers' news and phone numbers, and she finally locates Gatemouth Brown.
583.q: It was incredible. Honestly, I don’t remember how all the pieces of the puzzle came together. I know the great David Friedman from WWOZ... People were calling into the station

439.t: Israel as home and the pandemic spent in Rio
439.s: Israel is home; she describes Tel Aviv and says the Tiny Desk concert was filmed in Rio during the pandemic.
439.q: Yeah, Israel will always be home, there’s where I grew up, that’s where my mom and my siblings are, and I love it. I just spent one month there and it was incredible. I love Tel Aviv, my city. I love driving around on my scooter and I love being able to stop and go into the city, the city is right…

790.t: Post-Katrina recovery and tradition in New Orleans
790.s: Recovery is uneven, newcomers arriving, and the city doing things as they always were, with Topsy Chapman and Hank Leo.
790.q: Yeah, I think the inner city part has. The French Quarter obviously. The Central Business District. Those areas are back up. I think there are a lot of surrounding areas that are still hard hit. People are still — the Ninth Ward, the lower Ninth Ward, out in the east they still have a lot of houses…

226.t: Returning to the house after Katrina
226.s: The house survived Katrina; he has visited for a Nancy Wilson benefit and the Heritage festival but never got inside.
226.q: Even with Katrina. I’ve been back there a couple of times. It’s still standing, still there. It wasn’t completely destroyed, but I can see – along the side of the house, I noticed the water mark – how high the water came up to it. I was never able to find anybody home there for me to go inside.…
